items.title: [Bug]: DDGS native primp hang holds the GIL, defeating timeout and Ctrl+C

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

A `web_search` using the bundled `ddgs` provider can still hard-freeze the Hermes process after the 30-second thread timeout shipped in #52118.

The blocked call can enter native `primp` code while holding the Python GIL. In that state:

- `future.result(timeout=30)` cannot regain the GIL to raise `TimeoutError`;
- Hermes's interrupt loop cannot run;
- Ctrl+C / SIGINT and SIGTERM do not recover the process;
- only SIGKILL from another process terminates it.

This report was prepared from a local Hermes installation with account data, filesystem paths, search contents, session identifiers, and unrelated process details removed.

## Relationship to existing reports

This appears to be the unresolved overlap of:

- #29966 — concurrent DDGS searches hard-freeze in `primp`/libcurl, Ctrl+C immune;
- #36776 — a DDGS search can hang the shared agent loop indefinitely;
- #52118 — added a 30-second `ThreadPoolExecutor` wall-clock timeout.

#29966 was closed on 2026-07-13 as implemented by the timeout in #52118. The live reproduction below occurred on 2026-07-20, after that closure, on current Hermes code containing #52118.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: `v0.18.2 (2026.7.7.2)`
- Upstream commit before the local diagnostic patch: `3d7e1c5f4353b358f0d9c159c339c0b67dde4e0d`
- Python: `3.11.14`
- OS: macOS `26.5.2`, arm64
- Web backend: `ddgs`
- Installed `ddgs`: `9.13.0`
- Installed `primp`: `1.2.2`

The bundled DDGS plugin currently has no minimum safe version; its setup metadata says only `pip install ddgs`. Newer releases were available during diagnosis (`ddgs 9.14.4`, `primp 1.3.1`). The parallel-initialization deadlock was addressed upstream in deedy5/primp#142 and released through newer DDGS versions, but existing Hermes environments can remain on the vulnerable versions.

## Sanitized runtime evidence

The final session-specific log entry was:

```text
INFO tools.web_tools: Web search via ddgs: '[query redacted]' (limit: 5)
```

No matching provider completion, timeout warning, tool result, or later model call was emitted for that session.

After several minutes, the Hermes process was still alive with low CPU use but made no progress. A macOS process sample showed the active native stack inside:

```text
primp.abi3.so
  ...
  take_gil
    _pthread_cond_wait
```

The remaining Python control threads were also waiting in `take_gil`, condition variables, queues, or `waitpid`. This is consistent with native code preventing the interpreter thread that owns `future.result(timeout=30)` from reacquiring the GIL and observing its deadline.

Recovery attempts against only the affected Hermes CLI process:

```text
SIGINT  -> process remained alive
SIGTERM -> process remained alive
SIGKILL -> process terminated
```

No credentials, URLs, query text, user data, local paths, or session identifiers are included here.

## Why the current timeout is insufficient

`plugins/web/ddgs/provider.py` currently runs the blocking DDGS operation in a `ThreadPoolExecutor` and waits with:

```python
future.result(timeout=_SEARCH_TIMEOUT_SECS)
```

This works for a worker blocked in Python operations that release the GIL, such as `time.sleep()` or `threading.Event.wait()`. The regression test added with #52118 uses that kind of blocking behavior.

It does not protect the process when the native extension holds the GIL. The parent cannot execute the timeout branch or process an interrupt until the native call returns.

The review discussion in #37422 already notes the second limitation: an already-running Python thread cannot be force-killed. Even when the timeout fires, the native worker may remain inside the process.

## Expected behavior

- A stalled DDGS search must not freeze the Hermes process.
- The configured wall-clock deadline must still fire if native code holds the worker interpreter's GIL.
- TUI/gateway interruption should terminate the active DDGS operation promptly rather than wait for the full deadline.
- No orphaned DDGS worker should remain after timeout or interruption.

## Suggested fix

Run each DDGS search in a disposable spawned process rather than a thread:

1. Parent and worker exchange a small result/error envelope through a one-way pipe.
2. Parent polls in short intervals up to the wall-clock deadline.
3. Between polls, parent checks the thread-scoped `tools.interrupt.is_interrupted()` flag.
4. On timeout or interruption, terminate and reap the worker, escalating to kill after a bounded cleanup period.
5. Add regression tests for:
   - native code deliberately holding the child GIL;
   - prompt TUI/gateway interruption;
   - successful and error result envelopes through a real spawned worker;
   - no remaining child process after every exit path;
   - Windows and POSIX native-block fixtures.

A local proof-of-fix using this design passes the focused DDGS/plugin tests and the wider web-provider suite, and the exact formerly hanging search subsequently returned normally. I can submit that implementation as a PR if maintainers agree with the process-isolation direction.

items.title: [Feature]: Add session list density modes to Hermes Desktop
items.body: ## Problem or Use Case Hermes Desktop currently renders every session in the sidebar as a single compact row: semantic state dot plus session title. That maximizes density, but sessions with similar titles are difficult to distinguish without opening them. Agent conversations also differ materially from email: they can span hundreds of messages, use many tools, switch models, and move across git branches, so an arbitrary latest-message excerpt is often noisy rather than useful. The Desktop already has the necessary deterministic session metadata, but the sidebar does not offer a presentation mode that surfaces it. Related: #40768 proposes broad app-wide typography and density controls. This request is narrower: it controls the information density of Desktop session rows and does not scale message padding or typography across the application. ## Proposed Solution Add a renderer-local **Session list density** preference under **Settings → Appearance** with three modes: - **Compact** — current behavior: semantic state dot and session title. - **Comfortable** — title plus a single deterministic metadata line containing the last-used session model, message count, total tool-call count, and branch/workspace context where available. - **Detailed** — Comfortable plus a one-line preview of the initial user request. Detailed-mode preview behavior: - use the existing deterministic `session.preview` value; - normalize it to one line and keep it bounded; - omit it when the displayed title already falls back to that same preview, avoiding duplicate text; - do not refresh it from the latest message or generate an additional AI summary. All modes must preserve the existing working, waiting-for-input, background-process, and unread-completion indicators. Long metadata values should truncate without wrapping, and the virtualized list should use density-aware row estimates to avoid initial scrollbar jumps. The preference should remain Desktop-local persisted presentation state. This requires no backend schema change, API extension, recurring model call, or Dashboard change. ## Alternatives Considered - **Spacing-only density presets:** the current row is already close to the useful compact floor, so changing padding without changing information content offers little value. - **Latest-message preview:** latest user text can be as short as “continue,” while latest assistant or tool output can be extremely large and unstable during agent loops. - **AI-generated evolving subtitles:** potentially more semantic, but duplicates title generation and introduces model cost, latency, persistence, refresh, failure, and stale-summary concerns for a sidebar decoration. - **A separate density and subtitle setting:** more flexible, but creates unnecessary combinations before there is evidence that users need independent controls. ## Feature Type Other — Hermes Desktop UI ## Scope Medium (few files, < 300 lines) ## Contribution - [x] I'd like to implement this myself and submit a PR ## Debug Report (optional) N/A — this is a deterministic Desktop presentation feature and is not related to a runtime failure.

items.title: One-shot mode (-z) builds the agent without waiting for background MCP discovery — slow stdio servers are silently dropped

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Summary
`hermes -z` (one-shot) snapshots the tool registry **before** background MCP discovery finishes. Fast servers (e.g. a compiled binary like `mcp-grafana`) usually make it in; slower stdio servers (a Python-based MCP that takes 2-12s to import/boot) are **silently dropped** — the agent runs without their tools, with no error anywhere.

Worse: since the model never sees the tools, it sometimes refuses the task and sometimes **fabricates** a plausible answer as if it had called the tool.

## Where
- `hermes_cli/main.py`: `_should_background_mcp_startup` returns True for `command in {None, "chat", "rl"}` → discovery runs in the `cli-mcp-discovery` background thread.
- `hermes_cli/oneshot.py`: `run_oneshot` / `_run_agent` build `AIAgent` directly and never call `hermes_cli.mcp_startup.wait_for_mcp_discovery()` (unlike the interactive path in `cli_agent_setup_mixin.py`, which does).

## Repro
1. Configure two MCP servers in a profile: one fast binary + one `command: python -m some_server` that takes ~5s to boot.
2. `hermes -p <profile> -z "list the names of all tools you have"`
3. Only the fast server's tools appear. Calling `discover_mcp_tools()` synchronously before `run_oneshot()` in the same process makes all tools appear — confirming it's purely the missing wait.

## Suggested fix
Call `wait_for_mcp_discovery()` in `_run_agent` before constructing the agent (bounded by `mcp_discovery_timeout`, so a dead server still can't hang the one-shot).

## Related quirk
Under `-p <profile>`, `load_config()` resolves the **profile** config, so a `mcp_discovery_timeout` set via `hermes config set` (global) is not honored by profile runs — worth a docs note at least.

We're carrying a local build patch for this; happy to send a PR if useful.

items.title: Slack adapter: thread-context skips messages whose text lives in blocks/attachments (e.g. Grafana alerts)

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
## Summary
When the agent is @mentioned inside a Slack thread, the adapter builds thread context from prior messages — but only reads `msg["text"]`. Messages posted by alerting integrations (Grafana, etc.) carry their content in **blocks/attachments** with an empty `text`, so they're skipped entirely. The agent then answers something like "I don't see any incident description in this thread" while replying literally under the alert.

## Where
`plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py`, thread-context loop:
```python
msg_text = msg.get("text", "").strip()
if not msg_text:
    continue
```
The **main** message handler already falls back to `_extract_text_from_slack_blocks(...)` and attachments — the thread-context path just never got the same treatment.

## Suggested fix
Reuse the existing helper in the thread-context loop: when `text` is empty, try blocks via `_extract_text_from_slack_blocks`, then attachments (`text` / `fallback`).

We're carrying a local build patch for this; happy to send a PR if useful.

items.title: custom_providers + api_mode: anthropic_messages silently routes to /v1/chat/completions instead of /v1/messages — usage.input_tokens always 0

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary
 
With a `custom_providers` entry configured with `api_mode: anthropic_messages`, Hermes still sends the request in OpenAI Chat Completions shape (hitting `/v1/chat/completions`-style routing) instead of the Anthropic Messages shape (`/v1/messages`). This has been confirmed independently from both sides of the wire:
 
- **Client side (us, Hermes operator):** live debug patch in `agent/usage_pricing.py::normalize_usage`, right at the `mode == "anthropic_messages"` branch, logging the raw `response_usage` object passed into it. Result for a real one-shot call:
```
provider='custom' api_mode='anthropic_messages'
raw=Usage(cache_creation_input_tokens=0, cache_read_input_tokens=0, input_tokens=0, output_tokens=7)
```
`output_tokens` is correct, `input_tokens`/`cache_read_input_tokens`/`cache_creation_input_tokens` are always `0`, regardless of prompt length or caching state.
 
- **Provider side (Requesty, via their engineer Thibault):** confirmed that the raw response their router receives Hermes requesting is OpenAI-shaped:
```json
"usage": {
  "prompt_tokens": 10,
  "completion_tokens": 4,
  "total_tokens": 14
}
```
not the Anthropic-shaped fields Hermes is supposedly configured for:
```json
"usage": {
  "input_tokens": 10,
  "output_tokens": 4,
  "total_tokens": 14
}
```
i.e. **Hermes is calling the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint even though `api_mode: anthropic_messages` is set** for that custom provider.
 
This explains the symptom exactly: `normalize_usage`'s `anthropic_messages` branch reads `getattr(response_usage, "input_tokens", 0)` — since the underlying object only ever carries the OpenAI-style fields, `input_tokens` (and both cache fields, which don't even exist in the OpenAI shape) default to `0`. `output_tokens` apparently still gets populated somewhere along the way (unclear whether via a partial/implicit `completion_tokens` → `output_tokens` mapping upstream of `normalize_usage`, or some other shim) — but `input_tokens` never does.
 
Net effect: Langfuse/Hermes usage reporting always shows `input_tokens: 0` (and no cache read/write tokens) for every request through this custom provider, even though the underlying provider (Requesty) reports correct usage on its own dashboard and prompt caching is demonstrably working (~98–99% cache-hit rate visible provider-side).
 
## Config used
 
```yaml
model:
  default: vertex/claude-sonnet-4-6@europe-west1
  provider: requesty
  context_length: 1000000
  default_headers:
    HTTP-Referer: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com
    X-Origin-Title: Hermes
 
custom_providers:
  - name: requesty
    base_url: https://router.eu.requesty.ai
    api_key_env: REQUESTY_API_KEY
    api_mode: anthropic_messages
 
fallback_providers:
  - provider: custom:requesty
    model: bedrock/claude-sonnet-4-6@eu-central-1
 
delegation:
  model: vertex/claude-haiku-4-5@europe-west1
  provider: requesty
  api_mode: anthropic_messages
  reasoning_effort: low
```
 
Requesty's `https://router.eu.requesty.ai` endpoint does support genuine Anthropic-shaped `/v1/messages`-style responses when hit correctly (that's the whole point of `api_mode: anthropic_messages`) — the issue is that Hermes isn't actually sending the request that way for `custom_providers`, `api_mode` is effectively ignored for routing purposes even though it clearly changes which parsing branch `normalize_usage` takes.
 
⚠️ Side note for anyone finding this issue while debugging a similar symptom: we briefly tried "fixing" this by **removing** `api_mode: anthropic_messages` entirely, on the theory that it only affected usage parsing. That was wrong and made things much worse — without it, every single request (primary model and fallback) failed outright with `HTTP 404: 404 page not found` against `router.eu.requesty.ai`, i.e. `api_mode` *does* meaningfully affect request routing/shape, it's just not producing the Anthropic-shaped request+response pair it's supposed to. Re-adding `api_mode: anthropic_messages` and restarting immediately restored normal operation (just with the `input_tokens: 0` symptom again).
 
## Environment
 
- Hermes Agent: pinned image tag `v2026.7.1` (Hermes Agent v0.18.0, "The Judgment Release")
- Provider: Requesty EU router (`https://router.eu.requesty.ai`), models routed through it: `vertex/claude-sonnet-4-6@europe-west1` (primary), `bedrock/claude-sonnet-4-6@eu-central-1` (fallback), `vertex/claude-haiku-4-5@europe-west1` (delegation)
- Deployment: gateway mode, Docker
## Ask
 
1. Please look at how `custom_providers[*].api_mode` actually gets threaded through to the outbound request builder — right now setting it to `anthropic_messages` changes which parsing branch `normalize_usage` uses, but doesn't appear to change which endpoint/request shape is actually sent, so the two are out of sync for third-party OpenAI-compatible-but-Anthropic-capable routers like Requesty.
2. Separately: Requesty (cc @Thibaultjaigu, who's been helping debug this from their side, and who already has an open PR at #27908 adding Requesty as a first-class provider) would like to be added as a native provider rather than routed through the generic `custom_providers` path — happy to help test if that lands, since it likely sidesteps this whole class of problem.
Happy to provide more logs/repro steps if useful — the debug patch above can be reproduced trivially by adding a one-line log statement at the top of the `anthropic_messages` branch in `normalize_usage`.

items.title: Desktop startup waits on expensive rich status snapshot

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/dashboard
labels.description: Web dashboard / control panel UI (dashboard/, landing)

items.body:
## Description

Local Hermes Desktop startup waits for the rich public `/api/status` response after the spawned backend has already bound its socket.

`/api/status` intentionally builds a full operational snapshot. On a real multi-profile configuration it includes gateway/plugin discovery, session state, host configuration and profile topology. That work is useful for status consumers, but it is not required to prove that the freshly spawned local backend can service requests.

## Reproduction

Using an isolated `HERMES_HOME` with the same non-secret config/profile shape as a real installation, launch `hermes serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 0`, wait for the backend ready-file, then time the first authenticated readiness request and the first `/api/status` request.

Four-process median on Linux:

| Request | Median |
|---|---:|
| lightweight event-loop readiness probe | 85.7 ms |
| current `/api/status` | 2189.7 ms |

The current Desktop cold-start path waits for the second result before opening its WebSocket, adding roughly 2.1 seconds on this installation.

## Expected behavior

Local Desktop startup should use a minimal authenticated readiness contract that proves the new backend is responsive without changing or weakening the rich `/api/status` contract.

Compatibility requirements:

- keep `/api/status` unchanged and public;
- keep remote Desktop connections on `/api/status`;
- fall back to `/api/status` when a newer Desktop launches an older local runtime;
- keep local profile-pool backends on the same readiness contract;
- do not remove plugin discovery, session data, profile topology or any feature.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: current `main` at `456f18b19`
- Desktop: Electron
- OS: Linux

items.title: [Feature]: Config-driven channel/team-ID → profile routing (generic, cross-platform incl. port-bound platforms like Teams)

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Feature Description

Add a config-driven way to route an inbound message to a specific **profile** based on a stable channel/team/tenant identifier (Slack channel ID, MS Teams team ID, Discord guild ID, etc.), independent of platform and without requiring per-profile distinct bot credentials.

## Motivation

We run Hermes as the gateway/agent loop for a multi-tenant SaaS (KNET Elevate) — one gateway process per customer org (`multiplex_profiles: true`). We want to give individual **projects within an org** their own isolated profile (own `.env`, own LLM provider key — see #51603 for the related credential-scope bug we hit building this) so a project can use its own Anthropic/OpenAI/etc. key without affecting other projects or the org default.

Today, profile selection only works via:
1. The `/p/<profile>/` HTTP path prefix (`gateway/platforms/webhook.py`).
2. A profile bringing its own **distinct platform credentials** — e.g. its own Slack bot token — via `_start_secondary_profile_adapters` (`gateway/run.py:7174-7234`). This works today for platforms not in `_PORT_BINDING_PLATFORM_VALUES` (Slack, since it isn't port-bound).

Path (2) does **not** work for platforms that run their own port-bound webhook server per instance — e.g. **MS Teams**, which uses the Bot Framework and binds its own port (`plugins/platforms/teams/adapter.py`). Those platforms have no path to per-tenant profile routing today without spinning up a fully separate bot registration per profile, which isn't practical at our scale (one project could mean one Teams channel within a single team-wide bot install).

## Proposed Solution

A new config key (e.g. `profile_routing` or a per-platform `channel_profile_map`) that maps a stable channel/team/tenant identifier to a profile name, checked once per inbound message — before `SessionSource.profile` is stamped — at the natural chokepoint in each adapter's message-receive path (or centrally, if `source.chat_id`/`team_id` is threaded through before `_resolve_profile_home_for_source`, `gateway/run.py:14727-14740`).

```yaml
# example shape
profile_routing:
  slack:
    "C0123456": project-alpha
    "C0654321": project-beta
  teams:
    "19:abc@thread.tacv2": project-alpha
```

Behavior:
1. On inbound message, look up the platform + channel/team ID in the map.
2. If a match exists, resolve that profile's `HERMES_HOME` (config, skills, memory, `.env`-scoped secrets) for this turn — same isolation `_profile_runtime_scope()` already provides for multiplexed profiles.
3. If no match, fall back to current behavior (default/active profile).

## Alternatives Considered

- **Dedicated bot credentials per profile** (existing path (2) above) — works for Slack today, but requires a distinct bot app registration per profile and doesn't work at all for port-bound platforms like Teams.
- **`channel_model_map`** (#54601) — solves a different, narrower problem (routing *model choice*, with shared session/memory state). We need full profile isolation (distinct credentials, memory, skills) per tenant/project, not just a model default.

## Related Issues

- #51603 — credential-scope bug we hit building on top of profiles; needs fixing regardless of this feature.
- #54601 — declarative per-channel *model* routing; adjacent but solves a narrower problem (shared state, model-only).
- #19809, #13633 — platform-specific (Discord, Feishu) per-channel/group profile routing proposals; closed/narrower in scope. This proposal is intentionally generic across platforms and keyed on a stable channel/team ID rather than platform-specific concepts.
- #10143 — Telegram topic-to-profile routing; same shape, different platform, marked duplicate — suggests a generic cross-platform mechanism is the right level to solve this at rather than one-off per-platform proposals.

## Scope / Effort Estimate

Small-to-medium: new config schema entry, one dict lookup inserted at each adapter's message-receive point (or centrally if the identifying fields are threaded through earlier), and tests extending the existing multiplex-profile test coverage.

items.title: [Bug]: Auto-updater rewrites source under the live desktop backend - commit splice bricks the session (576 failures, 149 wasted API calls)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary

The git-install auto-updater rewrites `hermes-agent` source **while the desktop backend is live**, with no restart and no warning. Because `agent/conversation_loop.py` is imported lazily on the first API call, a process can end up running **two different commits spliced together** — one commit's `AIAgent` against another commit's `conversation_loop`. When the interface differs between those commits, every turn in the session fails permanently.

I hit this on a session that then failed **576 consecutive times over 39 hours**, burning 149 provider API calls against a deterministic, non-retryable `AttributeError`.

## Impact

- Any desktop session started shortly before an auto-update lands is silently bricked for its entire lifetime.
- The failure is permanent for that process — restarting the **gateway** does not fix it (I tried; the gateway is a separate process). Only a full desktop restart clears it.
- There is no circuit breaker: the loop retried a local `AttributeError` 149 times, each one a real provider call.
- The user-visible symptom is not an error message but a **wall of concatenated "thinking" labels**, because the method that crashes is the one that collapses interim status text (see below).

## Timeline of the actual failure

| Time (UTC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 2026-07-19 02:32:44/45 | Desktop + `serve` backend launch → import `run_agent` at commit `bd0021233` |
| 2026-07-19 02:33:03→04 | Updater: `reset: moving to HEAD` → `reset: moving to origin/main` = `19bf16c4d` — **19 seconds after launch** |
| 2026-07-19 02:37:56 | First API call lazily imports `agent/conversation_loop.py` → loads `19bf16c4d` bytes → **crash on API call #1** |
| 2026-07-20 17:28:58 | Later `pull --ff-only` to `456f18b19` (moves the call site 4948 → 4998) |

## The splice, proven

The two commits are each internally consistent. It is only the combination that is broken.

```console
$ git show bd0021233:run_agent.py | grep -c "def _interim_assistant_visible_text"
0
$ git show bd0021233:agent/conversation_loop.py | grep -c "_interim_assistant_visible_text"
0
```

`bd0021233` — loaded into memory at startup — neither defines nor calls the method. Coherent.

`19bf16c4d` — written to disk 19 seconds later — defines it at `run_agent.py:4820` and calls it at `agent/conversation_loop.py:` **4551, 4555, 4948, 4950**.

The traceback lands on **4948**, exactly:

```
2026-07-19 02:37:56,425 ERROR agent.conversation_loop: Outer loop error in API call #1
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../hermes-agent/agent/conversation_loop.py", line 4948, in run_conversation
    current_interim_visible = agent._interim_assistant_visible_text(assistant_msg)
                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'AIAgent' object has no attribute '_interim_assistant_visible_text'
```

## A diagnostic trap worth knowing about

After the later pull to `456f18b19` moved that call site from 4948 to 4998, the *same* error started rendering like this:

```
2026-07-20 17:51:29,552 ERROR agent.conversation_loop: Outer loop error in API call #141
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../hermes-agent/agent/conversation_loop.py", line 4948, in run_conversation
    # tool progress until the no-tool-call branch clears it at
                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'AIAgent' object has no attribute '_interim_assistant_visible_text'
```

**A comment under the caret.** `linecache` reads the *current* file to render source text while the interpreter executes the *old* code object. This is a reliable fingerprint of in-place source replacement — but it is also badly misleading: it makes the most recent update look like the culprit when the session had in fact been broken for 39 hours already. Worth surfacing in docs or in the error path.

## Why the UI shows a wall of text

`_interim_assistant_visible_text` is the routine that dedups/clears interim "thinking" labels. Because *that* is what throws, every retry appended a fresh label and nothing ever collapsed them. ~149 labels concatenated into one unbroken run of bold text in the transcript — so the visible symptom looks like model confusion rather than a crash.

Interim-output cleanup should run from a failure-safe `finally` path, not depend on the same state whose absence caused the failure.

## Reproducibility — the race is not rare

It re-fired on my very next launch:

```
a5b9803a5 HEAD@{2026-07-20 18:07:51 +0000}: pull --ff-only origin main: Fast-forward
456f18b19 HEAD@{2026-07-20 18:07:50 +0000}: reset: moving to HEAD
```

Desktop launched 18:06:35 → updater rewrote the tree **76 seconds later**. That one was harmless only by luck: `a5b9803a5` touches `agent/moonshot_schema.py` and two test files, leaving `run_agent.py` and `agent/conversation_loop.py` byte-identical. Same race, benign commit.

Two observed instances, 20s and 76s after launch respectively.

## Suggested fixes

1. **An updater must never mutate executable source beneath a live code-loading process.** This is the root cause; everything else is mitigation.
2. **Make "check for update" read-only.** "Apply" should either drain and restart every affected runtime (desktop `serve` *and* gateway), or stage for next start and surface "restart required".
3. **Expose the loaded generation per process** (commit/build stamp captured at import time), and refuse new work — with a clear message — when it differs from the installed tree. This turns a silent 39-hour brick into an actionable prompt.
4. **Circuit-break deterministic local exceptions.** `AttributeError`/`TypeError` from local code are not retryable; an identical exception signature repeating should break immediately and never trigger another provider call. 149 billed calls against an unrecoverable local bug is the worst part of this.
5. **Failure-safe interim cleanup**, per above.
6. **Checkpoint before any updater-directed restart**, and offer resumption after.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent **v0.18.2** (2026.7.7.2)
- Install method: **git** (`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`)
- Commits involved: `bd0021233` (in memory) / `19bf16c4d` (on disk) / `456f18b19` / `a5b9803a5`
- Python 3.11.15, OpenAI SDK 2.24.0
- Ubuntu 26.04 under WSL2, Electron desktop build
- Provider: `openai-codex`, model `gpt-5.6-sol`

Working tree was clean throughout (`git status --porcelain` empty apart from an untracked `.install_method`) — no local patches, no disk corruption. A full desktop restart resolved it; the error count froze and the session resumed normally with its history intact from `state.db`.

items.title: Cross-session prompt cache misses: per-session bytes sit ahead of the only system breakpoint

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P0
labels.description: Critical — data loss, security, crash loop

labels.name: sweeper:risk-caching
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break/degrade prompt caching or cache-key stability (invariant)

items.body:
# Cross-session prompt cache misses: per-session bytes sit ahead of the only system breakpoint

## Summary

The `system_and_3` caching strategy (`agent/prompt_caching.py`) places a single `cache_control` breakpoint at the **end** of the system prompt. Because Anthropic cache matching is all-or-nothing up to a breakpoint (over `tools → system → messages` in that order), any byte that differs between two sessions' system prompts forfeits the *entire* shared prefix — including the tool schemas and the large static head of the prompt that are byte-identical across sessions.

Hermes already keeps the prompt byte-stable **within** a session (evaluate-once, cached on `agent._cached_system_prompt`). But **across** sessions of the same profile/surface, the prefix is effectively always cold, even though most of it is identical.

## Where the divergence comes from (request-dump diff)

Diffing real `request_dump_*.json` bodies from two sessions on the same surface (identical tool schema set, byte-identical when sorted) shows the system prompts diverge within the first few hundred characters. The per-session offenders, in order of appearance:

1. **Skills index** — regenerates as skills are added/edited (differs across days).
2. **Workspace git snapshot** (`coding_context`) — branch/ahead-behind/status/recent-commits differ per session (`Branch: main → ahead 30` vs `ahead 1`).
3. **Volatile tail** — memory snapshot, user profile, date/model/provider line (already last, correctly).

The system prompt tiers are already built separately (`build_system_prompt_parts` → `stable`/`context`/`volatile` in `agent/system_prompt.py`) — but they are joined into one string with one trailing breakpoint, so the tiering currently buys nothing across sessions.

For any deployment where sessions of the same profile start within the cache TTL of prior activity (interactive multi-session use, gateways, cron fleets), each of those session starts pays a full cache write (1.25×/2×) for a prefix that is almost entirely shared, instead of a warm read (0.1×) — and loses the corresponding TTFT cut on the first turn.

## Proposal

Split the system message into two content blocks with an earlier breakpoint:

1. **Block 1 (static):** identity/SOUL, tool guidance, skills index, environment/platform hints — with its own `cache_control` marker. Identical for every session of a profile/surface until skills or identity actually change.
2. **Block 2 (per-session):** context files, workspace git snapshot, memory, external memory-provider block, date/model line — followed by the existing end-of-system breakpoint.

Breakpoint budget (Anthropic max 4): static block + end-of-system + **last 2** messages instead of last 3. The third message breakpoint is the least valuable of the four; the static block covers tools + the bulk of the prompt for every new session.

One content move is required: the workspace git snapshot is currently built into the *stable* tier via `coding_context` — it must move to the per-session block (it is stable within a session but never across sessions).

The Anthropic adapter already preserves `cache_control` markers on system content-block lists (`convert_openai_messages_to_anthropic`), so the adapter path needs little or no change. Envelope layouts (OpenRouter et al.) need the static-block marker placed on a content part, consistent with the `_can_carry_marker` rules from #57845.

## Related issues / prior art

- **#20880** — same breakpoint-budget problem seen from the tools side ("`system_and_3` skips tools schema", proposes `system_tools_and_2` / `cache_tools: true`). On native Anthropic the tools array is implicitly covered by any breakpoint *after* it, so an early static-block breakpoint resolves that report's core complaint too; a strategy/config knob could serve both.
- **#64167** (and RFC #58547, #50203, PR #51589) — establishes the evaluate-once/byte-stable system-prompt invariant for plugin-injected sections, but only *within* a session. This proposal extends the same invariant across sessions by isolating what cannot be cross-session-stable behind an earlier breakpoint.
- **#17476** / **#58813** — the live-time consolidation is already moving volatile time out of the cached prompt; this generalizes that direction to the workspace snapshot and memory blocks.
- **#12089** (closed) — sliding message breakpoints; different (heuristic, history-side) approach. This proposal is deterministic and prefix-side, so the concerns that closed #12089 don't apply.
- **#57845** — envelope-layout marker rules that the static block must respect.
- **#64103** / **#66127** — attack prompt *size* and history churn; complementary to prefix *ordering/breakpoints*, no overlap in mechanism.
- Side note for reviewers: with `prompt_caching.cache_ttl: 1h`, cache-write cost display is affected by **#43353** (1h 2× writes not representable in `PricingEntry`); unrelated to this change but likely to co-occur in testing.

## Expected impact

- New sessions start with a warm read of tool schemas + static prompt (typically tens of KB) whenever any session of the same profile ran within the TTL.
- Skill edits or identity changes invalidate only until the next session warms the new prefix; same-day sessions still share.
- Sessions with genuinely different tool sets (different surfaces) form their own cache populations, as today.

Happy to contribute the implementation (strategy change + `system_prompt.py` split + regression tests) if the direction is acceptable.

items.title: Cold Desktop resume + rotating preflight compression duplicates persisted transcript

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

On the first turn after a cold Desktop resume, legacy (rotating) preflight compression can append the entire already-persisted transcript to the parent session a second time before creating the continuation child.

This is durable SQLite duplication, not a renderer-only duplicate. Repeating restart/resume + threshold compression grows the parent transcript and makes future compactions slower and less reliable.

Tested at `c59ca4694` with `compression_in_place = false`.

## Reproduction

1. Create a session and persist at least two history rows.
2. Cold-resume it through the TUI/Desktop gateway so the stored rows are passed into `run_conversation()` as `conversation_history`.
3. Submit one new user turn while the restored context is already above the preflight compression threshold.
4. Let `_compress_context()` take the legacy rotation path.
5. Inspect the parent session in `state.db`.

Minimal invariant:

```python
db.append_message(parent, "user", "persisted question")
db.append_message(parent, "assistant", "persisted answer")
loaded = db.get_messages_as_conversation(parent)
messages = [*loaded, {"role": "user", "content": "new turn"}]
agent._persist_user_message_idx = len(messages) - 1
agent._compress_context(messages, "sys", approx_tokens=120_000)
```

## Actual

The parent contains:

```text
persisted question
persisted answer
persisted question
persisted answer
new turn
```

## Expected

The parent should contain the two existing rows plus only the newly accepted turn:

```text
persisted question
persisted answer
new turn
```

## Root cause

The normal turn flush receives `conversation_history` and skips those already-durable dicts by identity. But the legacy rotation branch in `agent/conversation_compression.py` currently calls:

```python
agent._flush_messages_to_session_db(messages)
```

Preflight compression runs before the normal turn flush has stamped the cold-resumed dicts. With no history boundary passed, `_flush_messages_to_session_db()` treats every restored row as new and appends all of them to the parent again.

## Proposed fix

Use `agent._persist_user_message_idx`, which `turn_context` anchors before preflight compression, to pass the already-durable prefix as `conversation_history`:

```python
current_idx = getattr(agent, "_persist_user_message_idx", None)
persisted_history = (
    messages[:current_idx]
    if isinstance(current_idx, int) and 0 <= current_idx <= len(messages)
    else None
)
agent._flush_messages_to_session_db(
    messages,
    conversation_history=persisted_history,
)
```

A regression test that pre-populates SQLite, cold-loads the transcript, appends one current user row, and forces rotating compression fails before this change and passes afterward.

## Verification

- New regression test passes.
- Full `tests/agent/test_compression_concurrent_fork.py`: 36 passed.
- No existing session/message IDs are modified; the change only prevents duplicate append on the boundary.

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state

items.body:
### Summary

With `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true`, these two helpers retain the first profile's `allow_private_urls` value in module-level state:

- `tools/url_safety.py::_global_allow_private_urls()`
- `tools/browser_tool.py::_allow_private_urls()`

A deterministic two-profile test currently produces `True, True` when profile A configures `true` and profile B configures `false`. The expected result is `True, False`. The reverse order also makes the first profile's value affect later profiles.

Confirmed on current `main` at `6fbb4cea00f8d7bcb80428c920a5db5f23d0768b`.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create two temporary profile homes with opposite `allow_private_urls` values.
2. Enter profile A using `set_hermes_home_override()` and call either helper.
3. Reset the context, enter profile B, and call it again.
4. Observe that the value from A is returned for B.

### Expected Behavior

Each helper follows the currently active profile configuration.

### Actual Behavior

The first value is reused for later profiles in the shared process.

### Root Cause

The two module-level caches are process-wide, while the active profile home is context-local. The underlying `read_raw_config()` reader is already cached by config path and file signature.

### Proposed Fix

When a profile-home override is active, read the setting from the active profile and rely on `read_raw_config()`'s existing path-aware cache. Keep the current process cache for ordinary single-profile calls.

I have the small fix and regression tests ready locally.

### Existing Work Checked

I searched open and closed issues, PRs, and commits:

- #24623 and PRs #24636 / #24641 / #24645 cover initialization ordering, not profile-specific values.
- PR #57624 covers cloud-browser credential lookup, not these setting caches.
- #65593 covers registry composition, not these helpers.
- #49693 / PR #49691 cover named browser sessions, not gateway profile configuration.

### Validation Prepared

- Two deterministic regressions fail before the fix and pass after it.
- 253 related synchronous tests pass.
- Ruff and `git diff --check` pass.

### Contribution

I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: Memory provider config reading broken — OpenViking and RetainDB cannot be enabled via Dashboard

labels.name: area/memory
labels.description: Memory subsystem: store, providers, sync, background reviews

items.body:
﻿### Bug Description

Two memory providers (OpenViking, RetainDB) fail to pick up non-secret configuration written by the Dashboard, making them impossible to enable through the UI. Additionally, all 8 in-tree memory providers implement config reading independently with no shared interface, leading to repeated bugs.

The root cause is on the **reading side**, not the writing side. `save_env_value()` already syncs to `os.environ` (config.py:8036), so secret fields work fine. The issue is exclusively with non-secret fields (endpoint, base_url, project) that are correctly saved to config.yaml but never read back by the provider's `is_available()` or `initialize()` methods.

---

### Steps to Reproduce

**OpenViking:**
1. Open Dashboard → Memory → OpenViking
2. Fill in `endpoint` (e.g. `http://localhost:8080`), leave `api_key` blank for local dev mode
3. Click Save
4. Dashboard shows "needs_config" — but `memory.openviking.endpoint` is correctly persisted in config.yaml

**RetainDB:**
1. Open Dashboard → Memory → RetainDB
2. Fill in `api_key`, `base_url` (e.g. `https://retaindb.example.com`), and optionally `project`
3. Click Save
4. Start a chat session that triggers RetainDB
5. `initialize()` calls `os.environ.get("RETAINDB_BASE_URL")` → empty, falls back to default → wrong server, despite base_url being present in config.yaml

---

### Expected Behavior

- `is_available()` should return `True` when config is properly saved, regardless of whether values were set via env vars or config.yaml
- `initialize()` should read non-secret config from config.yaml when env vars are not set
- All memory providers should share a common config reading path to prevent future inconsistencies

---

### Actual Behavior

**OpenViking** (`plugins/memory/openviking/__init__.py:1837-1848`):
`is_available()` only checks `os.environ.get("OPENVIKING_ENDPOINT")`. It never reads `memory.openviking.endpoint` from config.yaml unless `use_ovcli_config` is set. The existing `_resolve_connection_settings()` already has the correct fallback chain (env → ovcli → config.yaml → default) but `is_available()` doesn't use it.

**RetainDB** (`plugins/memory/retaindb/__init__.py:490-496`):
`initialize()` reads `base_url` and `project` exclusively from `os.environ`. These non-secret fields are written to config.yaml by the Dashboard, but the runtime never consults that file.

---

### Affected Component

- Configuration (config.yaml, .env, hermes setup)
- Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

---

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

- N/A (CLI only)

---

### Debug Report

N/A — this is a code-level bug, not a runtime error in my environment. All analysis is based on reading the source code on current `main`.

---

### Operating System

N/A (cross-platform)

---

### Python Version

N/A

---

### Hermes Version

Current main branch

---

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

**Root cause 1 — OpenViking (`plugins/memory/openviking/__init__.py:1837-1848`):**
`is_available()` duplicates the logic of `_resolve_connection_settings()` but misses the config.yaml fallback for `endpoint`. The fix is to replace the hand-rolled env check with a call to `_resolve_connection_settings(provider_config)`.

**Root cause 2 — RetainDB (`plugins/memory/retaindb/__init__.py:490-496`):**
`initialize()` treats all config fields as env-var-only. Non-secret fields should fall back to `memory.retaindb` in config.yaml when env vars are absent.

**Root cause 3 — No shared config reading interface across all providers:**

| Provider | Non-secret config source | Secret config source |
|---|---|---|
| **Honcho** | `honcho.json` host block → global → env | Same (dual-write to JSON + .env) |
| **Hindsight** | `hindsight/config.json` → env | Same (dual-write) |
| **Holographic** | Local-only (no external deps) | — |
| **ByteRover** | `config.yaml` (`memory.byterover`) | `os.environ` |
| **Supermemory** | `supermemory.json` | `os.environ` |
| **Mem0** | `mem0.json` + env overlay | `os.environ` |
| **OpenViking** | env → ovcli → config.yaml | `os.environ` (`is_available()` broken) |
| **RetainDB** | **`os.environ` only** (ignores config.yaml) | `os.environ` |

The saving path correctly separates secrets → `.env` and non-secrets → config.yaml / JSON. The bug is entirely on the reading side. `save_env_value()` already syncs to `os.environ` (config.py:8036), so secrets are fine — only non-secret fields in config.yaml are missed.

---

### Proposed Fix (optional)

**Short-term (fix the two broken providers):**
1. **OpenViking**: Change `is_available()` to call `_resolve_connection_settings(provider_config)` and check `settings.get("endpoint")` instead of manually inspecting `os.environ`
2. **RetainDB**: In `initialize()`, read `base_url` and `project` from `os.environ` first, falling back to `memory.retaindb` in config.yaml

Both fixes are small and localized (< 20 lines each). I can submit these as a PR.

**However, I believe the short-term fixes alone are not enough.** The deeper issue is that there is no canonical config reading interface for memory providers — each one implements its own ad-hoc logic, and new providers will inevitably repeat the same bugs.

**Before submitting any PR, I'd like the maintainers to clarify a standard practice:**
- Where should non-secret provider config be stored — config.yaml or a dedicated JSON file?
- What is the standard method for `is_available()` to check readiness?
- Should all existing providers be migrated to a uniform interface?

**I'm willing to implement both the short-term fixes and the unified config reading interface once a clear guideline is established. But without a documented standard, any fix I submit would be guesswork — and the next new provider will likely suffer from the same fragmentation.**

---

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: [Feature]: Expose Kilo Auto Efficient (kilo-auto/efficient) in the Kilo provider model picker

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:cannot-reproduce
labels.description: Sweeper: could not reproduce on current main

items.body:
## Feature Description

Add first-class visibility and selection support for Kilo’s Auto Efficient model-routing tier:

`kilo-auto/efficient`

Hermes already supports Kilo Code / Kilo Gateway as an inference provider. The Kilo gateway additionally exposes managed "Auto Model" tiers. Auto Efficient is a server-side routing model that chooses an underlying model per request based on task difficulty, session context, benchmark performance, and cost.

Hermes should surface this model in the Kilo provider picker and preserve it as a valid Kilo model ID through normal configuration, model switching, and fallback paths.

## Motivation

Today, a Hermes user can configure a fixed Kilo-backed model, but does not have a discoverable way to select Kilo’s managed cost-optimization tier.

Kilo Auto Efficient is useful for agent workloads because it:

- Routes routine work to a cheaper model.
- Upgrades difficult work, such as debugging or complex refactoring, to a more capable model.
- Is session-aware, avoiding needless model changes across related turns.
- Falls back to Kilo Auto Balanced when it cannot route confidently.
- Keeps its model mapping server-managed as pricing, availability, and benchmark results change.

This is especially appropriate for Hermes's long-running, tool-using sessions, where a fixed high-end model can be unnecessarily expensive for routine file inspection, small edits, or straightforward command execution.

## Proposed Solution

1. Add `kilo-auto/efficient` to Hermes's Kilo model inventory/curated fallback list so it is visible in the interactive model picker.

2. Ensure it is treated as a valid Kilo model ID everywhere a user-selected Kilo model travels:
   - `hermes model`
   - Config validation / `hermes doctor`
   - Session-level model switching
   - Kilo provider request construction
   - Fallback-provider normalization

3. Preserve the literal model ID sent to Kilo Gateway:

```yaml
model:
  provider: kilocode
  default: kilo-auto/efficient
```

4. Document that it is a Kilo-managed routing tier, not a pinned underlying model. The actual model serving a request may vary over time and within a session.

5. Optionally display the routed underlying model in Hermes footer/status output when Kilo returns that information in a response. This can be follow-up work if the API metadata is not already available.

Example:

```bash
hermes chat --provider kilocode --model kilo-auto/efficient
```

## Alternatives Considered

### Require users to hand-edit `config.yaml`

This is functional only if the ID already passes validation and is forwarded intact, but it is undiscoverable and does not meet the expected provider-picker experience.

### Implement a Hermes-side cost router

This would duplicate Kilo's continuously updated benchmark-driven routing, require maintaining routing policy and a model-cost catalog, and cannot use Kilo's own session-aware decisions. Hermes should delegate that responsibility to Kilo by selecting the gateway's managed model ID.

### Use a fixed low-cost Kilo model

That reduces cost but loses automatic escalation for harder tasks and the Balanced fallback.

## Scope / Effort Estimate

**Small** — primarily provider/model inventory, picker visibility, validation/normalization coverage, regression tests, and short provider documentation.

Likely areas:

- Kilo provider model inventory or curated fallback models
- Model picker / provider catalog
- Config validation and provider normalization
- Tests for picker visibility and outgoing model preservation
- Kilo provider documentation

## Additional Context

items.body:
## Bug Description

Hermes Desktop appears to hide or replace a substantive assistant response when a follow-up verification-only response is generated immediately afterwards.

This happened twice in the same desktop session. The agent first produced a long, useful, human-readable summary of completed work. Then a system-triggered verification instruction caused the agent to run a focused ad-hoc verification step and send a short verification summary. In the desktop UI, the earlier useful answer was no longer visible in the normal chat flow, and the user only saw the short verification message.

From the user's perspective, Hermes Desktop looked like it had replaced the real answer with boring verification boilerplate.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use Hermes Desktop on a coding task where the agent edits files.
2. Let the agent finish with a long substantive response, for example a detailed implementation summary with counts, findings, and file paths.
3. A post-turn system message says the workspace lacks fresh verification evidence and instructs the agent to create and run an ad-hoc verifier.
4. The agent runs the verifier and sends a short follow-up response focused on ad-hoc verification.
5. Observe the desktop chat view.

## Expected Behavior

The desktop app should preserve both assistant messages in order, or otherwise keep the substantive answer visible and accessible.

A later verification follow-up should not hide, replace, collapse, or visually supersede the previous answer.

Ideally, verification follow-ups should be visually attached as a small status/update under the original result, or shown as a normal additional message without making the original content disappear.

## Actual Behavior

The user reported that Hermes Desktop showed a long useful response briefly, then after the verification step the UI hid that response and only showed the short ad-hoc verification response.

The user had to ask the agent to repeat the full response because the detailed summary they were reading disappeared.

This happened at least twice in one session.

## Why This Matters

The verification follow-up is not the main deliverable. For real coding and data tasks, the valuable content is often the detailed summary: what changed, what was found, what files were written, what counts matter, and what decisions remain.

If the desktop UI effectively replaces that with verification boilerplate, the user loses the important result and the agent appears less useful.

## Concrete Example From Session

The task was a Patreon/shop audit workflow. The agent produced a detailed Phase 1 summary including:

- the generated audit queue files
- counts by recommended action
- Lucia Set 2 and Set 6 results
- top re-upload candidates
- name rewrite coverage such as `Pops -> Adrianna Floss` and `Becca -> WLRose`

Then a system-triggered verification prompt caused the agent to run an ad-hoc verifier and reply with only a short verification message. Hermes Desktop then appeared to show only the verification message, hiding the useful Phase 1 summary.

## Suggested Fix

Please check the desktop message rendering/update logic for cases where a later assistant message or post-tool verification turn replaces the previous assistant bubble.

Likely places to inspect:

- streaming message finalization
- message IDs or reconciliation keys reused across assistant turns
- post-turn verification or system-injected follow-up messages
- logic that treats the latest assistant response as an update to the previous response rather than a new chat item
- virtualization or collapsed message rendering in the transcript

## Environment

- Surface: Hermes Desktop app
- Host OS: macOS 26.4
- Active profile: photographer
- Context: coding task with file edits followed by system-triggered ad-hoc verification

## Notes

The agent can work around this by repeating the summary, but the UI should preserve the original answer automatically.

items.body:
## Symptom

When an agent run's message history contains a lone UTF-16 surrogate (e.g. `\udc97`), the run dies with:

``\'
'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udc97' in position N: surrogates not allowed
``\'

Observed with the `kimi-coding` provider (`https://api.kimi.com/coding`); the same workload on `openai-codex` completes fine, which suggests some provider paths sanitize message content before encoding and others don't.

## Context

- Lone surrogates enter message history when tool output contains bytes that aren't valid UTF-8 (read with surrogateescape), e.g. cp1252 smart-dashes in files or CLI output.
- Once present, the error also **snowballs inside cron error text**: each failed run embeds the previous error string, and the reported position grows run over run (observed: 5864 → 6670 → 7761 → 8712 → 9983).
- Triggered via a cron job on a profile whose model is kimi-coding. Fix attempt notes: after the job was pinned to openai-codex, the identical workload completed successfully.

## Suggested fix

Sanitize message/tool-output strings before encoding the provider request (e.g. `s.encode('utf-8', 'replace')` round-trip, or strip lone surrogates at tool-output ingestion). Sanitizing once at ingestion would also keep session stores clean.

## Evidence (redacted)

``\'
ERROR cron.scheduler: Error processing job <id>: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udc97' in position 8712: surrogates not allowed
provider=kimi-coding base_url=https://api.kimi.com/coding model=...
``\'

Happy to provide a minimal repro if useful.

items.body:
# Exponential conversation history doubling in Responses API (`_build_response_conversation_history`)

## Summary

When using the `/v1/responses` endpoint with `previous_response_id` chaining, the stored `conversation_history` doubles in size every turn. The user message is duplicated and the system prompt leaks into stored history. By turn 4-5, the payload exceeds the context window and the conversation crashes.

## Root Cause

`_build_response_conversation_history` in `gateway/platforms/api_server.py` has a fallback path that double-appends the user message when `turn_start` detection fails.

The real agent returns `result["messages"]` with a **system message as the first element**:

```python
result["messages"] = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "<system prompt>"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "4"},
]
```

But `_response_messages_turn_start_index` builds `expected_prefix` from `conversation_history + [current_user]` — which never starts with a system message. So the prefix comparison **always fails**, `turn_start` returns `0`, and the fallback runs:

```python
# Fallback path (line ~3892):
full_history = prior                          # loaded history
full_history.append(current_user)            # adds user message
full_history.extend(agent_messages)           # adds full agent_messages
                                               # (which ALREADY contains current_user)
return full_history
```

`agent_messages` already contains the user message, but the fallback appends it again separately. The system prompt also gets stored via `agent_messages`.

## Impact

Every turn, the stored history doubles. The user message and system prompt accumulate exponentially:

| Turn | User messages stored | System prompts stored | Total messages |
|------|---------------------|----------------------|----------------|
| 1 | 2× | 1× | 3 |
| 2 | 4× | 3× | ~7 |
| 3 | 8× | 7× | ~15 |
| 5 | 32× | 31× | ~63 |
| 10 | 1024× | 1023× | ~2000+ |

Consequences:
- **Context window exceeded** by turn 4-5 (~150-300K tokens)
- **Prompt cache invalidated** every turn (prefix changes due to duplication)
- **System prompt leaked** into `response_store.db` in plaintext
- **response_store.db bloat** — hits 100-response LRU limit in ~7 turns
- **Conversation crashes** — 404 when evicted response ID is requested, or 400 from context length exceeded
- **Cloud API cost** — exponential token usage, full-price on every turn (no cache hits)

## Existing Test Does Not Catch This

`test_previous_response_id_stores_full_agent_transcript_once` (line ~1951 in `test_api_server.py`) mocks `_run_agent` with:

```python
mock_run.return_value = (
    {
        "final_response": "2",
        "messages": [{"role": "assistant", "content": "2"}],  # ← no system message
        "api_calls": 1,
    },
    ...
)
```

The mock omits the system message, so `turn_start` detection succeeds in the test but **always fails in production** where the real agent includes the system prompt.

## Suggested Fix

Strip system messages from `agent_messages` before processing, and return `agent_messages` directly when `turn_start` fails (it already contains the full transcript):

```python
def _build_response_conversation_history(
    conversation_history, user_message, result, final_response,
):
    prior = list(conversation_history)
    current_user = {"role": "user", "content": user_message}
    agent_messages = result.get("messages") if isinstance(result, dict) else None

    # Strip system messages — the real agent includes the system prompt as
    # the first element, but the stored transcript must not contain it.
    if isinstance(agent_messages, list):
        agent_messages = [m for m in agent_messages if m.get("role") != "system"]

    if isinstance(agent_messages, list) and agent_messages:
        turn_start = APIServerAdapter._response_messages_turn_start_index(
            conversation_history, user_message, result,
        )
        if turn_start:
            return list(agent_messages)

        # turn_start failed — agent_messages already contains the full
        # transcript (prior + current_user + assistant). Return it directly
        # instead of double-appending.
        return list(agent_messages)

    full_history = prior
    full_history.append(current_user)
    full_history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": final_response})
    return full_history
```

Also update the test mock to include a system message so it reproduces the real-world scenario:

```python
mock_run.return_value = (
    {
        "final_response": "2",
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "What is 1+1?"},
            {"role": "assistant", "content": "2"},
        ],
        "api_calls": 1,
    },
    ...
)
```

## Verification

3-turn test with the fix applied:

```
Turn 1 → resp_599bcf05...
Turn 2 → resp_0d16a8c4...
Turn 3 → resp_658dabeb...

Turn 3 stored history (6 messages):
  [0] user: Turn 1 test message
  [1] assistant: I'm operational. Ready to query data.
  [2] user: Turn 2 test message
  [3] assistant: Ready.
  [4] user: Turn 3 test message
  [5] assistant: Ready.

→ User msgs: 3 (expected 3)
→ System msgs: 0 (expected 0)
→ Total: 6 (linear, not exponential)
```

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.18.2 (also confirmed on v0.19.0 / `origin/main`)
- Using `/v1/responses` with `previous_response_id` chaining and `stream: true`
- Backend: ollama-cloud (glm-5.2)

items.title: Desktop disk plugins disappear in remote gateway mode

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

items.body:
## Summary

Hermes Desktop v0.19.0 does not discover disk plugins while connected to a remote gateway. The loader combines the **remote backend's** `hermes_home` with the **local Electron filesystem** bridge, so the scan silently targets a path that cannot exist on the desktop machine.

## Reproduction

1. Put a valid plugin at `<remote hermes_home>/desktop-plugins/example/plugin.js`.
2. Connect Hermes Desktop on macOS or Windows to that remote gateway.
3. Restart Desktop or run **Reload desktop plugins**.
4. The plugin does not appear in the inventory or shell.

The same plugin loads in local connection mode.

## Root cause

`apps/desktop/src/contrib/runtime-loader.ts` currently does this:

```ts
const { hermes_home } = await getStatus()
const { entries } = await window.hermesDesktop.readDir(`${hermes_home}/desktop-plugins`)
```

In remote mode, `getStatus()` describes the remote backend, while `window.hermesDesktop.readDir` reads the desktop machine. For example, a remote path such as `/home/user/.hermes/desktop-plugins` is handed to local macOS/Windows. The broad catch around the scan hides the mismatch.

## Security boundary

The loader's own header correctly says runtime plugins execute with full renderer authority and that remote plugin source must not reuse this pipeline without a real boundary. Therefore, changing the scan to fetch plugin JavaScript from the remote filesystem would be unsafe.

The safe behavior appears to be:

- load trusted disk plugins from a **machine-local Desktop plugin directory**, independent of the active gateway's `hermes_home`; or
- explicitly show that local disk plugins are unavailable in remote mode.

A narrow Electron capability that returns/reads the local Desktop plugin directory would preserve the current trust model and file watcher.

## Expected behavior

Switching Local → Remote gateway should not make machine-local Desktop plugins disappear, and the loader should never combine a remote path with a local filesystem call.

## Suggested regression test

With a remote connection active and a remote status payload, assert that disk-plugin discovery either:

1. reads a deliberate local plugin root through Electron; or
2. reports the unsupported state;

but never calls the local filesystem bridge with the remote `hermes_home`.

items.title: Native session bridging: mirror one conversation across surfaces (desktop <-> Telegram)

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
### Problem / use case
A single user runs Hermes on one host and wants **one conversation visible and usable from
two surfaces at once** — the Electron desktop app *and* a platform DM (Telegram) — so they
can glance at either and see the same thread, and reply from whichever is at hand.

Today these are **separate session contexts**:
- A desktop chat spawns a local session (`tui_gateway.slash_worker`, its own session id, no
  `chat_id`).
- A Telegram DM is a distinct session bound to a `chat_id`; the gateway delivers that
  session's assistant turns only to its `<PLATFORM>_HOME_CHANNEL`.

There is no supported way to keep the two in sync. Observed constraints:
- No `mirror_session_to` / bridge configuration exists.
- The `msg.get("mirror")` path (`gateway/run.py:911`) tags a one-off cross-session delivery
  ("[Delivered from …]"), it is not continuous sync.
- Interactive desktop/telegram sessions live in the gateway's in-memory `SessionDB` and
  aren't persisted to `state.db` until session end, so an external DB watcher can't mirror a
  live session.
- The desktop *can* open a `watch=1` spectator window on a session id, but it is view-only,
  and desktop-typed input never appears as a message in the Telegram thread.

### Requested capability
A first-class **session bridge**: a config (or runtime binding) that designates a session
as mirrored to one or more channels, such that:
1. Assistant turns fan out to every bound surface (already partly possible via
   home-channel delivery).
2. **User turns entered on any bound surface are echoed to the others** (the missing half),
   e.g. a desktop-typed message surfaces in the Telegram thread as user input, and
   vice-versa — so both transcripts stay identical.
3. De-duplication is handled centrally (the gateway already suppresses duplicate final
   sends — see "Suppressing normal final send" log lines — which a bridge must cooperate
   with, not fight).

Sketch of a config shape:
```yaml
# per-session or per-profile
bridge:
  session: "agent:main:telegram:dm:8578391602"
  mirror_to:
    - desktop            # local Electron client
    - telegram:8578391602
  echo_user_turns: true  # the key ask — symmetric transcripts
```

### Why upstream (not a user-side bridge)
A user-side bridge must poll the private in-memory `SessionDB`, re-implement dedup, and
re-render markdown per platform — fragile and prone to break on internal changes. The
gateway already owns session state, home-channel delivery, and dedup, so it is the only
place this can be done robustly.

### Alternatives considered
- **Single-surface (Telegram primary) + desktop spectator window** — works today as a
  read-only mirror, but not symmetric (can't reply from desktop into the Telegram thread).
- **Custom external bridge** — rejected: private-API fragility, dedup complexity.

### Environment
- Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20), git install, macOS (Apple Silicon), always-on headless
  gateway.

---

*Filed by the fleet (J.A.R.V.I.S., Claude Code) for John. Companion to the operational
notes in work/BRIDGE_ADDENDUM.md and work/handoff-jarvis-gateway-analysis.md.*

items.title: Unguarded cross-module import makes releases non-atomic: ImportError TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT from agent.prompt_builder

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:cannot-reproduce
labels.description: Sweeper: could not reproduce on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
### Summary
`agent/system_prompt.py` imports symbols from `agent/prompt_builder.py` at module top
level, unguarded. When a release lands `system_prompt.py`'s import of a symbol **before**
`prompt_builder.py` defines it — or a user's working tree is pulled between those two
commits — the agent crashes on import with:

```
ImportError: cannot import name 'TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT' from 'agent.prompt_builder'
```

This repeatedly killed a headless gateway's morning-briefing cron until both commits were
present locally.

### Root cause
- `TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT` was introduced in commit `306e2d2`.
- `agent/system_prompt.py` imports it in a plain top-level `from agent.prompt_builder
  import (...)` block (still unguarded on upstream HEAD as of **v0.19.0** — confirmed via
  `git show HEAD:agent/system_prompt.py`).
- There **is** a `try/except` guard around the *usage*, but it does nothing for the
  *import* — an ImportError at the import line aborts module load before any usage guard is
  reachable.
- Verified: `git show HEAD~1:agent/prompt_builder.py | grep -c TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT`
  → `0`, while `system_prompt.py` at that same tree already imports it.

### Confirmed fix (running in production downstream)
We applied fix #1 below as a local stopgap on 2026-07-15; it has **survived the v0.19.0
update** (auto-reapplied by our updater) with zero recurrence. The exact patch:
```python
try:
    from agent.prompt_builder import TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT
except ImportError:
    TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT = ""  # optional Telegram rich-Markdown hint; degrade gracefully
```

Net: releases are effectively **non-atomic** across these two modules. Any window (CI
partial deploy, user `git pull` mid-range, an auto-updater pulling one file's commit
first) between the two commits yields a hard crash loop.

### Impact
- Headless / always-on deployments (LaunchAgent, systemd, cron) crash-loop on every agent
  spawn until the tree is fully consistent.
- Silent to the user except as repeated cron failures; recovery ("clear .pyc, hermes
  update, restart") appears to work but only because the second commit eventually lands.

### Suggested fixes (either or both)
1. **Guard the import** so a missing optional symbol degrades instead of crashing:
   ```python
   try:
       from agent.prompt_builder import TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT
   except ImportError:
       TELEGRAM_RICH_MESSAGES_HINT = ""   # fall back to base hint
   ```
2. **Enforce atomic releases** for coupled modules (single commit / release gate), so
   `system_prompt.py` never references a `prompt_builder.py` symbol that isn't shipped in
   the same revision.

Fix #1 is the durable safety net (protects users on any intermediate tree state); fix #2
addresses the release process itself.

### Environment
- Reproduced on Hermes Agent v0.18.2; **still unfixed upstream on v0.19.0 (2026.7.20)**.
- Install method: git, Python 3.11.15, macOS (Apple Silicon), headless gateway via
  launchd `KeepAlive`.

---

*Reported by the fleet (J.A.R.V.I.S., Claude Code) on behalf of John; diagnosis originated
with F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Hermes, fleet-mini). See work/handoff.md for the operational timeline.*
